newsitem.title: USA: Blue-chip stocks edge lower, pause after record highs.
newsitem.headline: Blue-chip stocks edge lower, pause after record highs.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks limped to a lower close on Friday as the market looked tired following this week's spirited run to a series of record highs on Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's comments about the economy.
The Dow Jones industrial average ended 3.49 points lower at 8,113.44, pausing after three straight record closes. For the week, the index was up 222.98 points.
In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,393 to 1,378 on moderate volume of 519 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
Analysts said the market appeared a bit fatigued but showed little indication that its broad, powerhouse rally was approaching a significant top.

"Quite frankly, I think we're due for a rest here," said James Crawford, senior vice president at Trevor Stewart Burton & Jacobsen Inc. "But I certainly don't think this a period when one has to run for cover."

There were pockets of nervous activity in the market, particularly among shares in personal computer makers. That group, which has rallied fiercely of late, saw its fortunes reverse after one of the companies, Gateway 2000 Inc., posted uninspiring earnings.
Gateway fell 2-11/16 to 40-1/2 and rival Dell Computer Corp. tumbled 7 to 163.
Analysts said they were not surprised at the severity of the group's fall, given investors' mercurial attitude to high technology stocks.
"We've seen them go through some pretty dramatic swings," said Ken Tower, technical analyst at UST Securities. "I don't think anyone is going to want to hold them for the ride down."
But the selling was narrowly focused and the technology-laden Nasdaq Composite index managed to scratch out a marginal gain, closing up 0.45 of a point to 1,569.58.
Investors will be tested next week, when a heavy diet of economic data will likely temporarily supplant quarterly corporate earnings on centre stage, at least temporarily.
Among the key data, are second-quarter Gross Domestic Product and employment cost index reports, the latter of which is a key benchmark for gauging nascent inflationary pressures in the economy.
Also on the calendar are monthly unemployment, wage and payrolls figures as well as the National Association of Purchasing Management index.

In the past, such a daunting week has often produced a timid if not fearful investor climate for Wall Street, but with this week's decidedly market-friendly testimony by Fed Chairman Greenspan still ringing in their ears, trepidation was hard to find among Wall Street professionals.
"He probably came as close as he's ever come to saying, 'Things look pretty darn good,'" Crawford said. "And in the big picture, things still do look pretty darn good."
Among individual issues, Dow component Caterpillar Inc. gained 1-13/16 to 56-13/16.
The maker of heavy equipment and machinery rallied after the U.S. Commerce Department reported durable goods orders rose a stronger than expected 2.3 percent in June.
Silicon Graphics Inc. jumped 5-7/8 to 25-5/16 after the high-end computer workstation maker reported stronger-than-expected fiscal fourth quarter earnings.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks fell 1.49 points to 938.79. The American Stock Exchange index edged up 0.75 to 637.80.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks fell 0.51 to 486.80. The average share was down 5 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 8,885.705 down 8.743 or 0.10 percent.
